title: The historical Chevron framework and its limits
shortTitle: The historical Chevron framework and its limits
summary: Chevron’s historical framework allocated some unresolved statutory questions to implementing agencies when their constructions were permissible. Loper Bright overruled that allocation.
notes:
The first step asked whether Congress had directly answered the precise issue. Courts used traditional interpretive tools to identify that answer and rejected contrary agency constructions. The second step applied when statutory silence or ambiguity remained: a permissible agency reading could govern even if the court preferred another reading. Chevron’s own dispute concerned EPA’s plantwide definition of stationary source. The casebook situates this formulation in the opinion’s context and explains that its later doctrinal influence exceeded the Court’s initially modest treatment of the case. (Printed 933–935.)

Later decisions determined the framework’s domain and effects. Mead asked whether Congress had delegated authority to act with the force of law and whether the agency interpretation exercised it; sufficiently formal procedures often signaled that authority. Brand X permitted a qualifying agency interpretation to displace an earlier judicial reading that had not found the statute unambiguous. King v. Burwell withheld deference on a question of extraordinary significance and independently adopted the agency’s interpretation. These examples show distinct threshold, precedent, and significance questions. (Printed 936–938.)

Loper Bright rejected the premise that ambiguity alone establishes delegation and required the court’s best interpretation. The assigned notes distinguish cases previously resolved at Chevron step one, discretionary policy choices under flexible grants, and former step-two disputes in which an agency had selected a permissible reading different from the court’s best one. The methodological change is clearest in that last category. Earlier decisions upholding specific agency actions remain subject to statutory stare decisis. (Printed 952–953, 963–966.)
